title: Oppenheimer's Gita quote originally 'I am time'

tellings.quote: reading that the original translation was not I am death the destroyer of worlds. It was I am time the destroyer of worlds.
Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom, The Slayer Time, Ancient of Days, come hither to consume;

plain: After the first atomic bomb test in 1945, Oppenheimer famously recalled a line from the Bhagavad Gita, the Hindu scripture: "I am become death, the destroyer of worlds." A guest named Dave Rossi, who says beings taught him advanced physics, tells Michels he read that the original translation was not "I am death" but "I am time, the destroyer of worlds." He does not say which translation he read. In Edwin Arnold's 1885 English translation, The Song Celestial, Krishna says at chapter 11, verse 32: "Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom, The Slayer Time, Ancient of Days, come hither to consume." That passage does speak of Time as the killer, as Rossi says, though in different words from "I am time, the destroyer of worlds." Rossi raises it because it gives the line a different sense: Oppenheimer's bomb as a turning of time rather than plain death.

discussion.by: The Song Celestial, or Bhagavad-Gita (translated by Edwin Arnold)
discussion.text: The teller does not say which translation he read; in Edwin Arnold's 1885 translation read here, Krishna's words at chapter 11, verse 32 are "Thou seest Me as Time who kills, Time who brings all to doom", which speaks of Time as the teller says, in other words than "I am time, the destroyer of worlds".
